headline: Low water on the Danube uncovers sunken warships

sources.title: Low water levels: EU clears old Nazi warships from the Danube
WWII German Warships Reappear as Danube Drought Exposes Wrecks in Serbia
Danube WWII wrecks cleanup boosts Serbia economy, environment
Sunken WWII ships emerge from Danube as river levels go down amid drought. #BBCNews (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen so low this summer that a sunken German [[fleet]] has {{shown up}} again near Prahovo, a town in eastern Serbia. Photographs published in late July 2026 show rusted [[hulls]] {{sticking out}} of the water along a [[stretch]] that boats normally {{pass over}} without seeing anything. The ships have been down there since 1944. What is different this year is that [[crews]] are finally {{pulling them out}}.

verbs.wrong: To move slowly down the river
verbs.why: Show up means something appears again after being hidden or forgotten for a long time. Old ruins can show up once a river drops to a record low level.

verbs.wrong: To lie on the river bottom
verbs.why: Stick out means part of something rises above a surface, like water, so you can see it clearly. The tops of sunken ships stick out once the river falls low enough.

verbs.wrong: To stop and dock at a port
verbs.why: Pass over means to travel above or across something without stopping. Boats normally pass over a hidden wreck without any sign it is there.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a place
verbs.why: Pull out means to physically remove something from where it has been stuck or resting. Crews use heavy equipment to pull out a wreck buried in mud.

chunks.text: In late 1944, the German navy was {{pulling back}} along the Danube as Soviet forces {{closed in}}. Rather than {{hand the ships over}} to the enemy, the crews sank about 200 of their own [[vessels]] near Prahovo, hoping the [[wrecks]] would block the river and {{hold up}} the Soviet [[advance]]. The plan lasted far longer than they [[intended]]. Eight [[decades]] later the hulls are still on the riverbed, and they have narrowed the safe [[channel]] from 180 meters to about 80.

verbs.correct: To leave when the enemy is near
verbs.wrong: To send more soldiers to a battle
verbs.why: Pull back means an army stops fighting and leaves an area because the enemy is close. Soldiers often pull back to a safer position before a battle ends badly.

verbs.correct: To get nearer on all sides
verbs.wrong: To stop and wait for orders
verbs.why: Close in means an enemy or a danger gets nearer from every direction at once. Soldiers can panic when they feel an army closing in on them.

verbs.correct: To give something to someone else
verbs.wrong: To hide something from the enemy
verbs.why: Hand over means to give control of something to another person or group. A defeated army might have to hand over its weapons and equipment.

verbs.wrong: To send a warning to the army
verbs.why: Hold up means to delay something so it happens later than planned. A single narrow channel can hold up river traffic for hours at a time.

chunks.text: That narrow channel costs Serbia about 5 million euros a year, because ships have to [[wait their turn]] to [[get through]]. Two boats passing each other can take [[anywhere from]] 40 minutes to four hours. [[Surveys]] with sonar and divers in 2021 {{turned up}} 38 wrecks in the worst section, and 21 of them are now being removed. The European Union {{put up}} a [[grant]] of 16.5 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, part of a project worth about 30 million. Divers {{clear away}} sand and silt with pumps before lifting gear takes each hull off the bottom. Some wrecks are too big or too [[fragile]] to move, so they are buried deeper instead, and others may still have [[ammunition]] on board.

verbs.correct: To find something after a search
verbs.wrong: To measure the depth of water
verbs.why: Turn up means something is found, often unexpectedly, after a search or an investigation. A sonar survey can turn up wrecks nobody knew were there.

verbs.wrong: To ask other countries for help
verbs.why: Put up here means to supply the money needed for a costly project. An organization can put up funds so builders have what they need to start work.

verbs.correct: To clean dirt or sand from a place
verbs.wrong: To mark a safe path for ships
verbs.why: Clear away means to remove dirt, sand, or objects so a space becomes clean. Divers slowly clear away mud before lifting equipment can reach a wreck.

chunks.text: The work is due to {{carry on}} until 2028. Serbia expects [[cargo]] on this part of the river to rise from 12.7 million tons a year in 2019 to 25 million by 2040, and one river ship can move as much grain as 120 trucks. Alessandro Bragonzi, who [[heads]] the European Investment Bank's office for the Western Balkans, said the project is an example of the kind of clean transport the bank wants to keep funding. In Prahovo, low water is [[an old story]]. The new part is that the ships people there {{grew up}} with may soon be gone [[for good]].

verbs.wrong: To change the plan for a project
verbs.why: Carry on means to continue with a task instead of stopping. Americans use it as well, but the phrase is heard even more in British English.
Grow up means to spend your childhood and become an adult in a particular place or way. People who grow up beside a river often feel a strong connection to it.

mainIdea.s: Low water on the Danube has uncovered dozens of German warships sunk near Prahovo in 1944. Crews are now removing the wrecks with European Union funding so ships can pass through more easily.
mainIdea.why: The article says the German fleet sank near Prahovo and crews are pulling them out with a 16.5 million euro EU grant.

mainIdea.s: Soviet forces sank about 200 ships in the Danube near Prahovo to stop the German retreat in 1944. Teams are now lifting the old wrecks so boats can use the full width of the river again.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the German navy sank its own ships to block the Soviet advance, not the other way around.

mainIdea.s: The Danube's record low water has cut electricity output at nuclear plants in Hungary and Romania this summer. Both countries have asked people to use less power to protect their reactors.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a separate energy crisis on the Danube, not about the sunken warships near Prahovo.
